paper_title: On the SPOT: Enhancing Speculative Decoding for Diffusion Language Models via Commit-Order Prediction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Diffusion language models (DLMs) promise parallel text generation, but in practice face an unresolved speed-quality trade-off. Exact decoding fills in only one masked position per model pass, while faster multi-token decoding schemes are lossy. Speculative decoding is the standard lossless acceleration for autoregressive models. However, it does not transfer directly to DLMs, which must choose both what to generate and where. We show that this order is the missing piece: the model's own predictions from the previous pass already give the right token at over $90\%$ of positions, but not which position comes next. We introduce Speculating Positions Order Trajectory (SPOT), a 0.62M-parameter model that reads only the target's output distributions, predicts this order and proposes a tree of candidate continuations, which the target verifies in a single pass by state equality. Coupled-noise match, which shares Gumbel noise between drafter and target, keeps this verification exact at any temperature. This approach also inspired us to introduce SPOT-Sets for dynamic threshold decoding, where a pass commits several positions: SPOT-Sets drafts whole commit sets together with their tokens. Our comprehensive experiments show that SPOT cuts target passes by up to $6.8\times$ and reaches up to $3.4\times$ the throughput of standard decoding on SDAR-8B, matching or beating the calibrated and training-free drafting baselines in every task and budget at $T=0$ and $T=1$. In addition, we show that SPOT's learned drafter transfers across models, demonstrating successful transfer across six different DLMs; with a light calibration, the SPOT-Sets drafter transfers as well. On top of dynamic threshold decoding, SPOT-Sets improves the throughput of SDAR-8B by 59% on average over the threshold decoder alone. Project page: https://eliezer318.github.io/SPOT-dLLM/

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Diffusion language models (DLMs) (Nie et al., 2025; Arriola et al., 2025) generate text by iteratively refining masked token sequences rather than predicting tokens left-to-right. Block-diffusion models make this particularly practical by combining bidirectional denoising within each block with causal generation across blocks (Arriola et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026). The diffusion paradigm enables new capabilities such as bidirectional attention, iterative refinement, enhanced safety robustness, and the potential to substantially accelerate language generation via parallel decoding (Ye et al., 2025; Rahimi et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). Yet this parallelism comes with fundamental speedquality trade-off. High-quality diffusion decoding typically uses conservative unmasking and therefore requires many denoising steps, while faster decoding schemes reveal multiple positions per step using confidence-based, top-k, or dynamic policies, potentially changing the decoding trajectory and degrading generation quality (Xu et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026). Our main setting is exact decoding with one commit per forward; we also address dynamic threshold decoding (Wu et al., 2026), which commits every position whose confidence clears bar. *Equal contribution. sections.content: Figure 1: SPOT overview (red: committed; amber dashed: drafted; grey: masked, with its stale (a) The target commits its most confident position per forward: argmax token). the tokens are largely known in advance, the order is not. (b) SPOT reads hypothetical prefixs stale distributions, predicts the next position with 0.62M order model, grows tree of states by prefix mass (edge width), and verifies all of them in one batched forward, committing three positions. For autoregressive language models (AR-LMs), speculative decoding provides an elegant lossless solution. cheap drafter proposes several future tokens, and the target verifies them in parallel while preserving exactly the distribution of draft-free decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). Recent work has begun bringing this idea to DLMs through self-drafting, draft graphs, learned residual predictors, and auxiliary draft models (Gao et al., 2025; Agrawal et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2025; Cui et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026). However, speculation changes fundamentally once attention inside block is bidirectional. In an autoregressive model, the next position is fixed, so the drafter only needs to predict what token comes next. In DLM, committing one position changes the representations and output distributions of all remaining masked positions in the block. The target must therefore decide both what token to write and where to write it next. Its future is not fixed sequence of token positions, but trajectory through partially filled block states. Several recent DLM speculative-decoding methods exploit this state-based view by proposing hypothetical future states and checking whether the target follows the same transitions (Gao et al., 2025; Agrawal et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026). This makes verification possible, but leaves two central questions unresolved: (Q1) what information should drafter predict to speculate several transitions ahead? and (Q2) how can tree of speculative states be verified exactly when the target samples rather than decodes greedily? Our key finding is that the main difficulty is not token prediction, but commit-order prediction. Over the speculative horizons relevant for acceleration, the targets stale distributions already provide strong token hypotheses: their top prediction matches the eventual committed token at 92100% of measured positions. Predicting which position commits next is considerably harder. This suggests reusing the targets stale token predictions while focusing the drafter on commit order, retaining additional high-probability token hypotheses when confidence is low. Based on this observation, we introduce Speculating Positions Order Trajectory (SPOT), lightweight 0.62M-parameter drafter that predicts future commit order from the targets stale output distributions (Figure 1). SPOT is prefix-conditional: after each hypothetical commitment, it predicts the next position again and organizes these predictions into tree of candidate block states, prioritizing high-probability branches. The target then evaluates the current and drafted states in single batched forward and accepts the longest prefix consistent with its trajectory. The second challenge is verifying speculative trees exactly when the target samples. Under greedy decoding, drafted transition is verified by comparing it with the targets next state. Under sampling, independent draws may disagree even when they come from the same distribution, causing state-equality verification to reject valid proposals. We address this with coupled-noise verification: the drafter and target share per-position Gumbel randomness, making the target transition deterministic conditioned on the shared noise. State equality can therefore verify an entire speculative tree, while marginalizing over the noise exactly recovers the targets sampling distribution. This enables exact tree-based verification at arbitrary tempera-

We draw inspiration from SPOT for dynamic threshold decoding, where target step commits set of positions. There the drafter must also choose the tokens, since the stale predictions miss more of the tokens of later steps (83% right one step ahead, 44% three steps ahead). SPOT-Sets still starts from the stale distributions, but drafts whole commit sets together with their tokens, also reading the targets hidden state and the candidates token embeddings, and grows tree whose nodes are whole target steps. The resulting method substantially reduces both model evaluations and wall-clock decoding time. On SDAR-8B, SPOT uses 1636% fewer target forwards than Spiffys calibrated draft graph and achieves up to 1.4 its throughput, with the adaptive-budget configuration reaching up to 1.7. Relative to standard draft-free decoding, SPOT reduces target passes by up to 6.8 and reaches up to 3.4 throughput. The gains hold across tasks at both greedy decoding and =1 sampling. We further evaluate on SDAR-4B, SDAR-1.7B and LLaDA2.0-mini, and test drafter transfer to two additional targets, LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B, covering six DLMs in total. On top of the threshold decoder, SPOT-Sets, with drafter trained on general chat only, raises SDAR-8Bs throughput to 5.29.9 that of standard decoding (7.9 on average), against 3.36.1 for the threshold decoder alone. Our main contributions are: We analyze speculative decoding for diffusion targets along drafting and verification axis, show that commit-order prediction is the drafting bottleneck while the targets stale distributions already supply the tokens, show why independent sampling breaks stateequality verification at > 0, and motivate coupling the drafter and verifier through shared randomness. Based on this analysis, we introduce SPOT, 0.62M-parameter prefix-conditional commitorder drafter that builds multi-step trees of block states from stale distributions, paired with coupled-noise verification, which provably preserves the targets distribution at any sampling temperature; inspired by SPOT, SPOT-Sets drafts the commit sets and their tokens for dynamic threshold decoding, with tree over whole target steps. We evaluate SPOT across tasks, temperatures, block widths and six diffusion language models: it beats or matches calibrated and training-free baselines in every setting at =0 and =1, cuts target passes by up to 6.8 on SDAR-8B, and its checkpoints transfer between models, including LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B, without retraining; on top of dynamic threshold decoding, SPOT-Sets reaches 7.9 the throughput of standard decoding on SDAR-8B on average, against 5.0 for the threshold decoder alone.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Speculative decoding and DLMs. Speculative decoding was introduced for autoregressive (AR) language models, where lightweight drafter proposes tokens that the target verifies in parallel while preserving its distribution (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). Later work improved the drafter with auxiliary decoding heads, learned drafters and dynamically built draft trees (Cai et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b;a; 2025), and complementary line uses diffusion models as drafters for AR targets (Christopher et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Ringel & Romano, 2026). Drafters accept more on the tasks they are trained on (Hong et al., 2025; Zbib et al., 2026) and lose speed under distribution shift (Wang et al., 2026), so we train our main SPOT-Sets drafter on general chat, not on the train splits of our benchmarks. DLMs instead generate text by denoising (Austin et al., 2021a; Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025); block-causal models such as SDAR make this practical block by block (Arriola et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026), while approximate caching and parallel unmasking accelerate decoding at cost in fidelity (Wu et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). Fast-dLLMs dynamic threshold commits every position whose confidence clears bar; SPOT-Sets (Section 4.4) speculates on top of this rule; with exact acceptance it leaves the output unchanged. Because attention inside block is bidirectional, the target decides not only what to write but where, so the commit order is an extra dimension of decoding and speculative decoding does not transfer directly. For verification we build on communication-free coupling: Daliri et al. (2025) show that two parties sampling from and under shared Gumbel noise agree with probability at least (1 DT )/(1 + DT ), and apply this to drafter-invariant speculative decoding. In contrast, our drafter learns the commit order, builds multi-step trees, verifies exactly under sampling, and transfers across targets without retraining; with SPOTSets it also drafts the commit sets of threshold decoding.

sections.title: 3 ANALYSIS OF BLOCK-DIFFUSION SPECULATIVE DECODING
sections.content: Setting. The target decodes block of masked positions one commit per forward (we write b32 for L=32). draft is hypothetical block state with few more positions filled by the drafter, and drafts are verified at once by appending each behind the cached prefix as its own copy of the block, so single forward over (1+D)L positions returns the targets next commit at the root and at every draft. draft is accepted iff it equals that commit at its parent, so the accepted set is one path and the output cannot change. draft therefore costs whole block rather than token: budgets are small, and target forwards (NFE) and wall clock diverge (Appendix D.2). Two measurements on SDAR-8B shape the method: what drafter must predict, and how its proposals must be verified once the target samples. 3.1 DRAFT-TRAJECTORY DYNAMICS Key Takeaway Knowing the future position order is almost as effective as knowing the full draft trajectory: the commit order carries most of the useful drafting information. draft must predict which position the target commits next and what token it writes. To isolate their value we evaluate live oracles that peek at the target continuation and propose (i) true positions filled with stale-argmax tokens, (ii) true tokens ordered by stale confidence, or (iii) both; each bounds the gain obtainable from one information source under standard verification.

sections.title: 4.4 SPOT-SETS: DRAFTING COMMIT SETS FOR THRESHOLD DECODING
sections.content: Faster decoders commit, in each forward, every masked position whose confidence cs(x) = maxv pθ,s(v x, C) clears bar τ , or the most confident one if none does (Wu et al., 2026). Given the shared noise G, this transition Φτ is still deterministic, so state-equality verification and Propositions 1 and 2 carry over to it. Inspired by SPOT, SPOT-Sets drafts its future steps, each whole set of positions whose tokens the stale argmax often misses (83/60/44% right one, two and three steps ahead; Appendix H.1). Its set drafter (5.1M parameters) therefore also reads the embeddings of the 16 most probable stale candidates and the targets last hidden state, and predicts for each position whether it clears τ at the next step and which candidate it takes. Tree nodes are whole steps, searched with the same prefix mass, floor γ and cap (SPOT-Sets-γ); draft that completes block also carries the next one (cross-block drafting), and the next blocks cache-refresh forward verifies drafts too (draft refresh; Figure 8). Training data. The drafter learns from the targets own threshold-decoded trajectories (τ =0.9, =0) on general chat prompts only, about 1M examples in all (Appendix H.1). The prompts are the first user turn of ShareGPT and UltraChat-200K (Ding et al., 2023) conversations, half from each, the datasets EAGLE-3 trains on (Li et al., 2025). Keeping the benchmarks own data out matters, since drafters accept more on the tasks they are trained on and lose speed under distribution shift (Hong et al., 2025; Zbib et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026); Appendix H.3 compares drafter trained on task prompts instead. Max-commit. Max-commit relaxes state equality and follows the accepted path with the most commits (Figure 3). Intuitively, its cut rule can only reduce the loss of threshold decoding, as it makes decoding stricter: it accepts drafted step only if it is the set higher bar τ τ would commit, step that stricter threshold decoder would also take. sections.title: 6 DISCUSSION
sections.content: DLM decoding remains constrained by fundamental speedquality trade-off. SPOT addresses this challenge with two-fold solution. We show that stale target distributions already contain highly reliable token information, making commit order the key missing signal for effective speculation. lightweight 0.62M-parameter model predicts this order and constructs multi-step draft trees, while coupled-noise verification preserves the target distribution under sampling; inspired by SPOT, SPOT-Sets drafts the commit sets and their tokens for dynamic threshold decoding. SPOT transfers across six DLMs without retraining, and on SDAR-8B it uses 1636% fewer target forwards than an offline-calibrated draft graph at up to 1.4 its throughput; there SPOT-Sets lifts dynamic threshold decoding from 5.0 to 7.9 the throughput of standard decoding on average, and from 4.8 to 6.8 at =1. More broadly, our results show that substantially faster DLM generation can be achieved without sacrificing the quality or exactness of the underlying decoding process (for SPOTSets, in its exact mode, or with the cut rule, which only makes the decoder stricter), establishing commit-order prediction as promising foundation for the next generation of speculative decoding methods for DLMs. Limitations. The main limitation of SPOT is that its gains diminish when verification is costly or acceptance is low. Verification becomes the bottleneck at wide blocks, while exact tree packing remains unresolved under bidirectional attention. Gains also narrow on low-acceptance tasks, and at 2 the =0-trained order model is outperformed by noise-aware ranking (Appendix F.7). SPOT-Sets reads the targets hidden states and token embeddings, so unlike SPOT it needs short calibration on each new target, and its larger drafter (5.1M parameters, about 6% of rounds time on SDAR-8B) matters more when the target forward is cheap.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: Generative AI tools were used during manuscript preparation to support language refinement and editing, and during development to assist with implementation of the experimental codebase. They were not used to formulate the research questions, develop the proposed method, define the evaluation procedure, or draw conclusions from the experimental findings. The quantitative results reported in this paper originate from the experiments described in Section 5.1 and the appendix. The authors inspected and verified all AI-assisted contributions, including code incorporated into the experimental workflow, and remain fully responsible for the manuscript, implementation, experimental results, and conclusions. ETHICS STATEMENT This work focuses on accelerating inference in diffusion large language models and does not involve human subjects or the collection of personal data. We do not anticipate any ethical concerns beyond those associated with the underlying language models and their downstream applications. REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT Code and the trained drafter checkpoints are available at https://github.com/ Eliezer318/SPOT-dLLM, with instructions to reproduce the experiments. Every number in the benchmark tables comes from one benchmark run with the protocol of Section 5.1 and Appendix D, on machines with eight identical NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell cards and one job per card. sections.content: D.1 DRAFTER TRAINING DETAILS Architecture: three-layer transformer encoder over the masked positions, dmodel=128, 8 heads, top32 stale probabilities per position (mtop=32), the stale runner-up as second token candidate (the hedge) when the top-1 probability is below 0.6; 0.62M parameters. Inputs per masked position: stale top-32 probabilities (raw and log), eight summary statistics, two path features (taken-position set, depth). Training data: decoding trajectories of the target itself at =0, with prefix-conditional examples extracted at every (round, depth). The prompt pools are recorded per shard and differ by target. The SDAR-8B b32 and LLaDA2.0-mini b32 drafters are trained on CodeAlpaca (Chaudhary, 2023) alone, 21k and 14k trajectories; the SDAR-4B drafter on four-pool mixture of CodeAlpaca, UltraChat (Ding et al., 2023) and the chat and code shards of the Llama-Nemotron post-training corpus (Bercovich et al., 2025), 15,027 trajectories. No pool contains MATH-500 or any evaluation sample. Optimization: Adam, learning rate 3104, 10 epochs; the released SDAR8B b32 checkpoint reaches 0.75 held-out next-commit accuracy (0.77 at depth 0, 0.72 at depth 7). Training drafter takes under two GPU-hours on one card. The identical procedure (data regenerated per target and width) produces the checkpoints for SDAR-8B b32/b16, SDAR-4B, SDAR-1.7B and LLaDA2.0-mini b32/b16; no per-setting tuning.

Two consequences follow, disclosed rather than controlled. The SDAR-8B and mini drafters have seen only code, while two of the four evaluation tasks are mathematics: their GSM8K and MATH500 runs are out of domain for the drafter, which makes those results evidence that the learned order carries across domains rather than memorizing one. And because the SDAR-4B drafter was trained on different mixture, any difference between the SDAR-8B and SDAR-4B tables confounds target scale with corpus composition; we report both and attribute neither. Regenerating the SDAR-8B corpus would invalidate every downstream run of the benchmark, so the confound is left in place and stated here. D.2 DRAFT LAYOUT AND VERIFICATION COST target forward at block state yields distribution at every masked position; the most confident position is filled and the block is re-run. To verify drafts in one forward, each draft is appended behind the cached prefix as separate copy of the block with its own mask layout, and copy attends to the prefix and to itself only, so its logits are exactly what the target would compute at that state. One forward over (1+D)L positions therefore returns the targets own next commit at the root and at every draft, rejected draft costs positions but never changes the output, and packing tree into single sequence is not exact here, since copys logits depend on its complete mask layout. D.3 DECODING CONFIGURATION Strict single-commit decoding (the threshold decoder of Section 4.4 for SPOT-Sets), generation length 256 (64 and 512 in Appendix F.5), block width 32 (16 where stated), exact prefix KV cache on (for LLaDA2.0-mini: an exact prefix-KV path we added to the released model code, verified to reproduce the uncached decoders commits), drafts laid out as copies of the block appended behind the prefix with blockwise mask, no padding of drafted forwards (every drafted run is unpadded), and each run records whether its configuration is distribution-preserving. Prompt templates and stopping rules per task are those of the released harness (Appendix E). D.4 BASELINE CONFIGURATION Spiffys draft graph is calibrated with the released procedure of Agrawal et al. (2026) (offline collection on held-out prompts: MBPP train and MATH500 problems disjoint from the evaluation samples, 25 each, lookahead 6, graph size 24) separately for SDAR-8B, SDAR-4B, SDAR-1.7B

SimSD (Cui et al., 2026) drafts with same-family sibling model and verifies the drafted tokens in one forward under plug-in attention mask that lends them temporally valid contexts. That test approximates the sequential denoising distribution instead of reproducing it, and its reported speedups come with changed (on average improved) generation quality. It is therefore lossy accelerator, not lossless speculative decoder, and its throughput is not commensurable with that of the exact methods compared here; we do not compare against it. MRP, from reported numbers. MRP (Xu et al., 2026) trains three-layer residual head to extrapolate the backbones logits up to K=3 denoising steps ahead and keeps drafted token where the backbones argmax agrees with it. It reports results on the same SDAR-Chat 1.7B, 4B and 8B targets and the same four tasks as this paper (its Table 2: block width 16, greedy decoding, one H100), against one-token-per-step baseline, which is the draft-free decoder of Section 3. The two are measured in different implementations, so the comparison is between relative gains: SPOT is ahead in all twelve settings, by 1.83.2, and uses 3.24.9 fewer target forwards than draft-free decoding, quantity MRP does not report. I.1 TERMS Stale conditionals. The most recently available target conditionals at the masked positions of block. They are stale because hypothetical future commitments change the true target distribution, but no additional target forward is performed while drafting (Section 4.2). Commit order. The sequence of positions the target commits next, one per forward under exact decoding. The drafter predicts it as qϕ(s y), distribution over the targets next committed position given hypothetical state (Section 4.2). Draft tree. Candidate block states grown by recursively querying the prefix-conditional predictor, high-probability branches first, up to budget of drafted states that the target verifies in one batched forward (Section 4.2).

Verification at > 0 in which the drafter applies the same Gumbel noise as the target, so that, conditioned on the noise, the target transition is deterministic and verification reduces to state equality (Section 4.3). SPOT (Speculating Positions Order Trajectory). The method: 0.62M-parameter order model, three-layer transformer encoder over the targets stale distributions at the masked positions, predicts the targets next committed position; its predictions grow draft tree that the target verifies in one batched forward (Section 4). SPOT-γ. SPOT with prefix-mass floor γ that discards candidates below it, so that the realized verification budget adapts to drafter confidence; calibrated per target, γ = 0.02 on the SDAR targets and 0 on LLaDA2.0-mini (Section 4.2, Appendix D.5). NFE and throughput ratio. NFE is the number of target forward passes per sample; the throughput ratio is measured against the draft-free run of the same task, model and temperature on the same machine; within 5% we say that two methods match (Section 5.1, Appendix D.8). Dynamic threshold decoding. The decoding rule of Fast-dLLM (Wu et al., 2026): each forward commits every masked position whose confidence is at least τ , or the most confident one if none is (Section 4.4). Commit set. The positions one threshold step commits; SPOT-Sets draft node is whole step.

sections.content: SPOT-Sets-γ. SPOT-Sets unpadded, with calibrated mass floor γ and cap of drafts, drafting across blocks, draft refresh, and max-commit with the product rule; SPOT-Sets-γ, exact keeps state-equality acceptance. Its drafter is trained on general chat prompts. Max-commit. relaxed acceptance rule for threshold decoding that may accept drafted step that is not exactly the targets set; it changes the output. I.2 COMMON QUESTIONS What problem does SPOT solve? SPOT accelerates diffusion language models without changing their output distribution. Exact decoding fills in only one masked position per model pass, while faster multi-token schemes are lossy. Speculative decoding is the standard lossless acceleration for autoregressive models (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023), but DLM must choose both what to generate and where. SPOT drafts several future commitments with small learned model, and the target verifies all of them in single pass (Section 1). Why is commit order, not the token, the bottleneck? The tokens are largely known in advance; the order is not. The stale argmax matches the true token in 92% of first-block commits and 90% thereafter, while the probability that the previous rounds top-confidence position commits next drops to 3% by the ninth block. Live oracles show that true positions are worth more than true tokens on every task (Section 3.1, Figure 2). How does SPOT draft and verify? SPOT reads the targets stale top-32 probabilities at each masked position, predicts the next committed position, and repeats the prediction after each hypothetical commitment to grow tree of block states. The target evaluates the current and drafted states in one batched forward and accepts the longest prefix consistent with its own trajectory. The drafter is trained entirely from draft-free target trajectories and uses no target hidden states, token embeddings or text (Section 4). Is the output exact when the target samples? Yes, for targets with an exact prefix cache. At = 0, state-equality verification reproduces the draft-free target trajectory for any drafter (Proposition 1). At > 0, the drafter and the target share per-position Gumbel noise, following the coupling of Daliri et al. (2025); conditioned on the noise, the target transition is deterministic, and the drafted output equals the draft-free output for every draw of the noise (Proposition 2). Draft quality therefore affects speed, never correctness (Section 4.3). How does SPOT differ from Spiffy, SSD and BlockSpec? Spiffy calibrates static draft graph offline (Agrawal et al., 2026), SSD orders positions by confidence into self-drafted chain (Gao et al., 2025), and BlockSpec-style tree ranks positions by the targets stale confidences (Pan et al., 2025); SPOT learns the commit order instead. Under one decoder and verifier, SPOT uses 1636% fewer target forwards than Spiffys calibrated graph at 1.041.41 its throughput on SDAR-8B, in every task and budget (Section 5.2). Which models and benchmarks does the paper use? The headline target is SDAR-8B (Cheng et al., 2026), dense block-causal DLM at block width 32. Drafters are also trained for SDAR-4B, SDAR-1.7B and the mixture-of-experts LLaDA2.0-mini (Bie et al., 2025), and transfer is measured on LLaDA-8B (Nie et al., 2025) and Dream-7B (Ye et al., 2025). The benchmarks are GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021b), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) and MATH500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021), with = 350 samples (all 164 for HumanEval) at generation length 256, except where caption says otherwise; Table 2 and Table 1 are the mean of seeds 02, the other tables seed 0 unless their caption says otherwise (Section 5.1). What are the main results? On SDAR-8B, SPOT needs 3.24.7 fewer target forwards than draft-free decoding at budget 8 and 4.16.8 at budget 20, at 2.53.4 the throughput at budget 8. At = 1 it keeps 1635% fewer forwards than Spiffy at 1.081.37 its throughput. On top of dynamic threshold decoding, SPOT-Sets reaches 5.29.9 the throughput of standard decoding at = 0 and budget 8 (7.9 on average), against 3.36.1 (5.0) for the threshold decoder alone. SPOT beats or matches every baseline in every setting at both temperatures (Sections 5.2, 5.3 and 5.4).

sections.content: Does SPOT work beyond SDAR-8B? Yes, across six DLMs. The same recipe gives the lowest NFE and highest throughput in every comparison on SDAR-4B; on SDAR-1.7B, and on LLaDA2.0mini, which has different tokenizer, it gives the lowest NFE in every comparison and beats or matches every baseline in throughput. The LLaDA2.0-mini checkpoint, pointed at SDAR-8B without retraining, costs 48% more forwards and still beats every baseline calibrated there. Checkpoints that never saw LLaDA-8B or Dream-7B cut their 256 forwards to 5588 and 5180, measured with an approximate prefix cache, so these rows measure reach rather than losslessness (Section 5.4). What does SPOT-Sets add, and is it exact? Faster DLM decoders commit every position whose confidence clears bar τ (dynamic threshold decoding). There drafted step is whole set of positions with token for each, so SPOT-Sets drafts commit sets and their tokens from the targets stale distributions, its hidden state and the candidate tokens embeddings, and grows tree whose nodes are whole steps. With state-equality acceptance (exact) the output is the threshold decoders own, up to floating-point batch effects. Max-commit with the product rule also accepts drafted step whose tokens are the targets top choices and whose confidences have geometric mean of at least τ ; it commits more per forward and changes the output, so its accuracy is reported next to the exact rows (Section 4.4, Appendix H). On SDAR-8B at = 0 and budget 8, SPOT-Sets-γ takes 47 48% fewer forwards than the threshold decoder at 1.571.62 its throughput; its exact variant still reaches 1.481.54  (Table 2)  . Its drafter is trained on general chat prompts. drafter trained on the task prompts is faster on those tasks (8.2 on average on SDAR-8B); the general chat drafter keeps 8797% of that drafters speed-up on GSM8K, MATH500 and MBPP, and 9799% on HumanEval, which neither drafter saw (Tables 27 and 28). What are the limitations? The gains diminish when verification is costly or acceptance is low. Verification becomes the bottleneck at wide blocks, and exact tree packing remains unresolved under bidirectional attention. Gains also narrow on low-acceptance tasks, and at 2 the order model trained at = 0 is outperformed by noise-aware ranking. SPOT-Sets needs short calibration on each new target, its larger drafter (5.1M parameters) matters more when the target forward is cheap, and its main rows use max-commit, which changes the output (Section 6). Where are the code and the drafters? The code, the trained drafters and the instructions to reproduce the experiments are at https://github.com/Eliezer318/SPOT-dLLM under the MIT license, and the drafters are mirrored on Hugging Face at https://huggingface. co/EliezerS/SPOT-dLLM (Appendix G). I.3 WHERE THIS WORK SITS SPOT brings speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) to diffusion language models (Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025), in particular to block-diffusion models that denoise within block and generate causally across blocks (Arriola et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026). It is compared against speculative decoding for DLMs with self-drafting, draft graphs and confidence trees (Gao et al., 2025; Agrawal et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2025), and verifies with Gumbel coupling (Daliri et al., 2025).
